opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's one of the things I find most interesting and most uncertain. When we think about what it would take for AI systems to meaningfully accelerate AI research itself, a lot of people focus on the parts that are easy to measure: can the model write the code, debug the training run, implement the paper? Models have gotten pretty good at those well-specified engineering tasks. But much of what makes a senior researcher valuable is something more like taste. Knowing which experiment is worth running. Noticing that a result is weird in an interesting way rather than a boring way. Knowing when to abandon a direction and when to push through.

The tricky thing is that taste is hard to evaluate. With a coding task you can check whether the tests pass. With taste, the feedback loop is long and noisy. You might only find out months later whether a research direction was good, and even then it's confounded by execution and luck. So it's hard to build benchmarks for it, and it's plausibly hard to train for, because you don't have a clean reward signal.

That said, I'd be cautious about assuming taste is some special, ineffable human thing that models will never have. Some of it is probably pattern-matching over a huge amount of experience: you've seen a lot of experiments, you have intuitions about what tends to work. Models have read an enormous amount of research, so in some sense they might have a broad prior about this. What they often lack right now is the grounded experience of running things, seeing them fail, and updating. As agents run more experiments autonomously over longer horizons, they might start accumulating something like that.

From an evaluation and risk perspective, I think the important question isn't "do models have taste, yes or no," but "how much does a lack of taste actually bottleneck progress?" If you can run a thousand mediocre experiments cheaply, maybe you can brute-force past some of the need for great judgment. Or maybe taste is the binding constraint and that doesn't work. I genuinely don't know, and I think it's one of the more important empirical questions for forecasting how quickly AI R&D automation could happen. So I'd like to see more effort on measuring it directly, even imperfectly, for example by having models propose research directions and seeing how experts rate them, or how they pan out when actually executed.

r001.rationale: The response describes taste as judging which experiments or directions are worthwhile and having intuitions about what tends to work, but does not clearly characterize it as predicting experimental outcomes.

r002.rationale: It says models may have a broad prior from reading research, but attributes current gaps to lacking grounded experience; it does not suggest limitations may come from failing to elicit existing capabilities.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss how many examples training would require or suggest that few examples could elicit existing knowledge.

r004.rationale: It contrasts verifiable coding tasks with taste’s long, noisy feedback, but does not explain that a task with a verifiable final outcome can require intermediate judgments without direct verification signals.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, partly because it's one of the places where I feel least confident about my own predictions.

When people say "scientific taste," I think they're bundling together a few different things. There's the ability to pick good problems, meaning knowing which questions are tractable and important rather than just interesting-sounding. There's the ability to notice when a result is suspicious, when something is too clean or the experiment doesn't actually test what you think it tests. And there's this harder-to-pin-down thing where an experienced researcher can look at a research direction and go, "no, that won't work," and they're right, and they can't fully articulate why.

My rough view is that current models are surprisingly decent at the first two in a shallow way and quite bad at the third. If you ask a frontier model to critique an experimental design, it'll often catch real problems. It'll flag confounds, it'll point out that your baseline is weak. That's genuinely useful. But if you ask it to generate a research agenda, you tend to get something that looks like the median of what's been published. It's plausible, it's well-formatted, and it's not the thing a good researcher would actually do next.

And I think that's partly a training data story. Good taste is mostly learned from feedback on your own bad ideas over years, and that feedback loop isn't really in the pretraining distribution. What's in the distribution is finished papers, which are the survivors, so you see the outputs of taste without seeing the process.

The thing I'd push back on, though, is people who are confident this is some kind of permanent limitation. At METR, a lot of what we do is try to measure how long and how messy a task can be before models fall over, and that frontier has been moving faster than I expected. Taste might just be what long-horizon agency looks like when the horizon is "a research career." If a model can run experiments, see them fail, and update, then it's getting the feedback loop that humans get, just compressed. I don't know if that produces something that deserves to be called taste, but I'd be nervous betting against it.

The part that worries me is that we don't have great evals for this. It's easy to measure whether a model can implement a known method. It's much harder to measure whether it picked the right method to try, because the ground truth for "was this a good research bet" takes months to arrive. So we might get models with real scientific taste and not notice for a while, or get models that are confidently wrong in ways that are hard to catch because they sound like good researchers. Both of those seem bad from a safety standpoint, for different reasons.

r001.rationale: The response describes choosing important, tractable problems and spotting suspicious results, but does not propose that scientific taste consists largely of predicting experimental outcomes.

r002.rationale: It attributes current weaknesses partly to missing feedback from failed ideas and allows that models may improve with experience. It does not suggest that the limitations reflect a failure to elicit capabilities the models already have.

r003.rationale: The response does not claim that selecting promising research ideas requires few examples or that this would elicit knowledge models already possess.

r004.rationale: It says evaluating research choices is difficult because the ground truth takes months to arrive, but does not explain that a verifiable final outcome can coexist with intermediate judgments that lack direct verification signals.

astra-6.text:
I think scientific taste is a bundle of things that are worth separating. There’s recognizing whether an idea is interesting, judging whether it’s likely to be true, and deciding whether working on it is actually a good use of your time. You could be very good at one of those and quite bad at another.

For models, I’d want to distinguish being able to give a convincing critique of a research proposal from being able to choose a direction and make progress on it. A model might tell you, very eloquently, why a question is important. But does that judgment predict which projects will produce useful results? That’s the thing we need to measure.

And it’s a difficult thing to measure because the feedback is slow and noisy. A good research decision can lead to a dead end. A fairly unimaginative project can succeed. So I’d be cautious about inferring either that models have great scientific taste from a few impressive suggestions, or that they lack it because lots of their suggestions are bad. Human scientists generate lots of bad ideas too.

The stronger test would be to give a model some resources, let it choose among research directions, and see what it discovers. Ideally, you’d look at that across many projects, including whether it notices when its original approach isn’t working and changes course. That seems much closer to the capacity we actually care about.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes judging whether an idea is likely true from judging its interest or value, but does not say scientific taste largely consists of predicting experimental outcomes.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes critique from choosing and pursuing a research direction, but does not suggest that apparent limitations may come from failing to elicit capabilities models already have.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss training models to select ideas, example counts, or eliciting existing knowledge.

r004.rationale: It notes that research feedback is slow and noisy, but does not explain that a verifiable final outcome can depend on intermediate judgments lacking direct verification signals.

sol-6.1.text:
I think scientific taste is quite hard to measure, because part of what you’re asking is whether a model can identify a question that we don’t already know is a good question. If you evaluate it by asking scientists whether they like the proposed research, you may be measuring how well it reproduces their preferences, rather than whether it can find something surprising and important.

I’d want to distinguish generating plausible research ideas from choosing which ideas are worth spending resources on. A model might be very good at producing a hundred interesting directions, but the valuable thing is knowing which one to pursue, what experiment would actually distinguish the hypotheses, and when to give up.

My guess is that models can learn a lot of that. I don’t see a principled reason why scientific taste would be inaccessible to them. But I’d be much more persuaded by a model making consequential research decisions, getting feedback from experiments, and consistently producing useful discoveries than by its ability to give a compelling explanation of why an idea is promising.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses identifying valuable questions and choosing experiments, but does not say that scientific taste largely consists in predicting experimental outcomes.

r002.rationale: It suggests models may learn scientific taste, but does not attribute apparent limitations to a failure to elicit capabilities they already have.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not discuss how many training examples idea selection might require or say that selection elicits existing knowledge.

r004.rationale: The candidate mentions consequential research decisions and experimental feedback, but does not explain that intermediate judgments lack a direct verification signal even when the final outcome is verifiable.
